hints: Focus on what homolytic fission means, one bond splits evenly so each atom keeps one electron to form two radicals.
List the three different bonds in $\text{CH}_2\text{BrCl}$ as $\text{C-H}$, $\text{C-Cl}$ and $\text{C-Br}$, and recall which is the weakest and longest.
Think about which bond needs the least energy to break, then work out which carbon fragment is left behind when that halogen leaves as $\text{Br}^\bullet$ or $\text{Cl}^\bullet$.
walkthrough:
**Understand homolytic fission**

Think of it like a tug of war ending in a draw. One covalent bond breaks and one electron goes to each side, giving two radicals.

General rule:
$$\text{X-Y} \rightarrow \text{X}^\bullet + \text{Y}^\bullet$$

**List the possible bonds to break**

In $\text{CH}_2\text{BrCl}$ the carbon is bonded to H, to Br and to Cl. Breaking just one bond gives three possibilities:
$$\text{CH}_2\text{BrCl} \rightarrow \text{ }^\bullet\text{CH}_2\text{Cl} + \text{Br}^\bullet$$
$$\text{CH}_2\text{BrCl} \rightarrow \text{ }^\bullet\text{CH}_2\text{Br} + \text{Cl}^\bullet$$
$$\text{CH}_2\text{BrCl} \rightarrow \text{ }^\bullet\text{CHBrCl} + \text{H}^\bullet$$

**Pick the weakest bond**

Bond strength decreases down the group because atoms get larger and overlap gets poorer. So the order is:
$$\text{C-Br} < \text{C-Cl} < \text{C-H}$$ in strength.
That means the $\text{C-Br}$ bond needs the least energy and breaks most easily.

**Identify the most likely radical**

Breaking the weakest $\text{C-Br}$ bond leaves the carbon still attached to the two H atoms and the Cl atom. That fragment is $^\bullet\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$, the most likely radical to form.

options.A: Correct. Breaking the weakest bond, $\text{C-Br}$, by homolysis gives $\text{Br}^\bullet$ plus the carbon radical $^\bullet\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$. This needs the least bond dissociation energy, so it is most likely.
options.B: Not likely. This would form by breaking the $\text{C-Cl}$ bond. The $\text{C-Cl}$ bond is shorter and stronger than $\text{C-Br}$, so it needs more energy and is less likely to break first.
options.C: Not likely. This would form by breaking a $\text{C-H}$ bond. $\text{C-H}$ is the strongest bond here, so homolysis to give $\text{H}^\bullet$ needs the most energy and is very unlikely under normal initiation.
options.D: Incorrect formula. $^\bullet\text{CH}_2\text{BrCl}$ would have five bonds to carbon, which is impossible. Homolytic fission must remove one atom, so the radical fragment must have one fewer atom than $\text{CH}_2\text{BrCl}$.
